index_record.dataset_generation_caption:
The figure presents a comparative schematic of two neural network architectures: Feedforward and Generative, illustrating their distinct processing flows for encoding and decoding. The overall layout is divided into two vertically aligned columns within a rounded rectangular boundary. The left column is labeled 'Feedforward' at the bottom in bold gray text, with a citation '(e.g., Serre et al., 2007)' beneath it. The right column is labeled 'Generative' similarly, with the citation '(e.g., Lee & Mumford, 2003)' below. A vertical red label on the left side reads 'Encoding (recognition)', while a vertical blue label on the right side reads 'Decoding (generative)', indicating the functional roles of each processing direction.

Each column contains four horizontal layers, represented as rectangular boxes, each containing six evenly spaced empty circles symbolizing neurons or units. In the Feedforward column, red upward-pointing arrows connect each layer to the one above it, indicating a unidirectional flow from bottom to top, representing the encoding process. There are no downward connections.

In contrast, the Generative column includes both red upward arrows (same as in Feedforward) for encoding and additional blue downward-pointing arrows connecting each layer to the one below it, representing the decoding or generative process. These blue arrows run parallel to the red ones but in the opposite direction, forming a bidirectional pathway between layers.

The visual modules consist solely of these rectangular layers with circular units and directional arrows. The red arrows signify recognition/encoding pathways, while the blue arrows denote generative/decoding pathways. All elements are rendered in black outlines except for the colored arrows and labels. The figure emphasizes the architectural difference: Feedforward models process information strictly in one direction (bottom-up), whereas Generative models allow for bidirectional processing, enabling feedback from higher to lower layers. This distinction reflects different computational theories of vision—feedforward for recognition and generative for reconstruction or prediction.
